common_name: Rojo Brillante Persimmon (Spanish Astringent Kaki, CO2-Treated 'Sharon Fruit' Type)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Rojo Brillante is astringent until de-astringed, so home growers should either wait for fruit to soften fully on the tree or hasten ripening with a brief CO2 or high-proof-alcohol treatment before eating firm.

directions: Rojo Brillante is Spain's dominant commercial persimmon cultivar, grown at enormous scale around Valencia under the Ribera del Xúquer designation and marketed internationally after a brief post-harvest carbon-dioxide treatment strips the astringency while the flesh stays crisp and apple-firm rather than jelly-soft, a trait that sets it apart from most other de-astringed kaki types. Fruit is large, deep orange-red, and glossy, with a thick skin that ships and stores unusually well for a persimmon. The tree is vigorous and productive, bearing reliably on second-year wood, and its relatively low chill requirement makes it a strong fit for Gulf Coast winters that rarely deliver much cold. Growers without CO2 treatment equipment can still enjoy the fruit by letting it soften completely on a windowsill, at which point the astringency resolves into rich, honeyed sweetness like any other soft-ripe persimmon.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Persimmon Production Guide
California Rare Fruit Growers — Persimmon Fruit Facts
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Jindai is non-astringent and self-fruitful, producing seedless fruit that can be eaten firm without a pollinator tree.

directions: Jindai is a Japanese non-astringent (PCNA-type) persimmon prized for its naturally compact, semi-dwarf growth habit, making it one of the easier kaki cultivars to keep manageable in a home orchard or even a large container without heavy pruning. Fruit is medium-sized, round to slightly flattened, orange-skinned, and virtually seedless when grown without a pollinator, and can be eaten crisp like an apple straight off the tree since it never develops the mouth-puckering tannins that afflict astringent types. The tree bears young and reliably, tolerates the mild winters of the Gulf South on modest chill accumulation, and its smaller stature makes netting against birds and squirrels considerably more practical than on full-sized persimmon trees. Fall color is a attractive bonus, with foliage turning shades of yellow-orange before the bright fruit hangs on bare branches into late autumn.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Persimmon Fruit Facts
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Persimmon Production Guide
Louisiana State University AgCenter

common_name: Aizumishirazu Persimmon (Seedless Japanese Astringent Kaki for Drying)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Aizumishirazu is astringent until fully soft or dried, so peel and hang firm fruit to air-dry into hoshigaki-style dried persimmon, or wait for full softening before fresh eating.

directions: Aizumishirazu hails from the Aizu region of Fukushima Prefecture and is one of Japan's classic astringent persimmon cultivars grown specifically for drying into anpogaki and hoshigaki, traditional sweet dried persimmon treats made by peeling and air-curing the firm fruit until the sugars concentrate and the tannins mellow. Fruit is medium-sized, conical, and seedless without pollination, with deep orange flesh that turns amber and jammy once fully soft for fresh eating instead of drying. The tree is a reliable, heavy annual bearer and handles the Gulf Coast's mild winters and modest chill hours without difficulty, though its astringency at harvest means growers should plan on either drying racks or a patient windowsill-ripening routine rather than eating fruit straight off the branch. Vivid orange fall foliage and heavily laden bare branches in late autumn make this a strong ornamental as well as a productive fruit tree.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Persimmon Fruit Facts
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Persimmon Production Guide
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Tenjin-gosho is astringent and seedless without pollination, so let fruit soften fully on the tree or indoors before eating, or peel and dry it like other astringent kaki types.

directions: Tenjin-gosho is a historic seedless astringent cultivar from Nara Prefecture, Japan, valued for large, elongated, acorn-shaped fruit with a distinctive pointed tip and deep orange color once fully ripe. Because it sets fruit without a pollinator and stays seedless under normal Gulf Coast growing conditions, the flesh softens evenly all the way through, giving smooth, honey-sweet pulp once astringency resolves rather than the harder pockets sometimes found in seeded types. The tree is vigorous, spreading, and productive, tolerating the region's mild winters on low chill accumulation, and the oversized fruit makes an especially striking specimen hanging on bare branches after leaf drop. Home growers can eat it soft and spoon-ripe, or peel and air-dry it into a dense, chewy dried persimmon in the same tradition as other astringent Japanese cultivars.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Persimmon Fruit Facts

common_name: Sui Jujube (Historic USDA-Chico Introduction, Small Round Chinese Date)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun in any well-drained soil; Sui sets a heavier crop when a second jujube cultivar such as Li or Lang is planted nearby, though it can also produce fruit on its own.

directions: Sui is one of the original jujube selections brought into the United States through the USDA's early-1900s plant introduction program and trialed at the Chico, California experiment station alongside Lang, Li, So, and Silverhill, making it one of the oldest named jujube cultivars still in American cultivation. Fruit is small to medium, round, and sweet with a crisp, apple-like texture when harvested at the mahogany-brown stage, and it dries into a wrinkled, date-like fruit if left to fully mature and shrivel on the tree. The tree shares the species' extreme drought tolerance and indifference to poor, alkaline, or compacted soils that defeat most other fruit trees, and it shrugs off Gulf Coast summer heat and humidity with essentially no disease pressure. Its long history in American orchards makes it a useful genetic and flavor comparison point alongside the more commonly planted modern jujube cultivars.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Jujube Variety Trials
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Jujube Production
California Rare Fruit Growers — Jujube Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Wiki Tu is a strong, reliable pollen source and pairs well with Kakariki, Anatoki, or other New Zealand cultivars to boost fruit set on both plants. Established plants tolerate brief dips to around 15-18F, making them reliable in zone 8 and zone 9.

directions: Wiki Tu is a New Zealand-bred feijoa cultivar developed as part of the modern wave of Kiwi selections aimed at improving on the older American-market standards like Mammoth and Triumph, prized both for good fruit quality and for its reliability as a cross-pollinator. Fruit is medium-large, oval, and smooth-skinned with sweet, aromatic flesh and a moderate seed count, ripening in the mid-season window typical of New Zealand feijoa breeding lines. The shrub is vigorous and heavy-flowering, and its abundant, well-timed pollen makes it a favored partner cultivar for other New Zealand-origin feijoas in mixed plantings, improving yields across the whole hedgerow rather than just its own fruit set. Like other feijoas it thrives on Gulf Coast heat and humidity once established, tolerating brief winter cold snaps and needing only routine watering and an annual light prune to keep its evergreen form tidy.
sources: New Zealand Institute for Plant and Food Research — Feijoa Variety Notes

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Kakariki sets a heavier crop with a distinct cultivar such as Wiki Tu or Anatoki planted nearby for cross-pollination. Established plants tolerate brief dips to around 15-18F, making them reliable in zone 8 and zone 9.

directions: Kakariki takes its name from the Maori word for the small native green parakeet, a nod to the deep green skin the fruit keeps even at full ripeness rather than showing the pale or bronzed blush some other feijoa cultivars develop. Fruit is medium-sized and oblong with sweet, fine-grained, aromatic flesh that ripens in the mid-to-late season, and the shrub itself is compact and well-branched compared to older, ranker-growing feijoa cultivars, making it easier to keep tidy in a smaller garden or as a clipped hedge. It flowers heavily in spring with the typical showy white-and-crimson feijoa blossoms, whose sweet fleshy petals are edible and popular with foraging gardeners. Give it full sun and good drainage, and expect the toughness and low-maintenance character typical of the species once past its first year or two of establishment.
sources: New Zealand Institute for Plant and Food Research — Feijoa Variety Notes
California Rare Fruit Growers — Feijoa Cultivar Selection

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Anatoki benefits from cross-pollination with a distinct cultivar such as Wiki Tu or Kakariki for the heaviest crop. Established plants tolerate brief dips to around 15-18F, making them reliable in zone 8 and zone 9.

directions: Anatoki takes its name from the Anatoki River valley in New Zealand's Golden Bay region, an area known for feijoa breeding, and produces medium to large, rounded fruit with thin skin and rich, sweet, aromatic flesh typical of the newer wave of dessert-quality New Zealand selections. The shrub grows with a naturally rounded, well-filled habit that needs less corrective pruning than older, leggier feijoa cultivars to look good as either a specimen or an informal hedge. Its spring flowers are abundant and showy, drawing pollinators for the fruit set as well as offering sweet, edible petals as an incidental garden snack. As with all feijoas, give it full sun, well-drained soil on the acidic side, and steady moisture through summer for the best fruit size, and expect it to shrug off Gulf Coast heat and humidity that would stress less heat-tolerant fruiting shrubs.
sources: New Zealand Institute for Plant and Food Research — Feijoa Variety Notes

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Robert is self-fertile and can crop as a single plant, though fruit set and size improve with a second cultivar nearby. Established plants tolerate brief dips to around 15-18F, making them reliable in zone 8 and zone 9.

directions: Robert traces to South American feijoa stock and has long been grown in California as a dependable self-fertile cultivar, meaning a single bush can set a worthwhile crop without a second variety planted for cross-pollination, a real advantage for gardeners with room for only one feijoa. Fruit is medium in size with smooth skin and sweet, juicy flesh carrying the classic pineapple-guava-mint flavor, ripening across a fairly long mid-season window rather than all at once. The shrub is a strong, reliable grower with the typical silvery-backed evergreen foliage, taking well to hedging, screening, or espalier against a sunny wall. Because it is self-fertile but still improves with a partner, gardeners who later add a second cultivar such as Wiki Tu or Anatoki nearby will usually see a further bump in yield and fruit size on both plants.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Feijoa Cultivar Selection

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Gemini sets fruit more heavily with a distinct cultivar planted nearby for cross-pollination. Established plants tolerate brief dips to around 15-18F, making them reliable in zone 8 and zone 9.

directions: Gemini is a compact-growing feijoa selection popular with home orchardists working in smaller garden spaces or large containers, staying noticeably more restrained in height and spread than rangier older cultivars while still producing good-quality, sweet, aromatic fruit. Fruit is medium-sized and egg-shaped with smooth skin and juicy, low-grit flesh, ripening in the typical mid-to-late season window shared by most feijoa cultivars. Its dense, naturally rounded evergreen habit makes it a strong choice for hedging or foundation planting where a full-sized feijoa would eventually crowd its neighbors, and the sweet, showy spring flowers are as much an ornamental draw as the autumn fruit crop. Give it full sun, consistent summer moisture, and a light annual prune to keep the canopy open and fruit accessible for harvest.
sources: New Zealand Institute for Plant and Food Research — Feijoa Variety Notes

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Den's Choice fruits more heavily when a distinct cultivar is planted nearby for cross-pollination. Established plants tolerate brief dips to around 15-18F, making them reliable in zone 8 and zone 9.

directions: Den's Choice is an Australian feijoa selection valued by home orchardists for consistently large, well-flavored fruit on a vigorous, heavy-cropping bush, making it a favorite in warm-climate feijoa plantings outside its native New Zealand breeding grounds. Fruit is oval to oblong with smooth skin and sweet, aromatic, moderately seeded flesh, ripening in the typical autumn window for the species. The shrub grows upright and dense with the characteristic gray-green, silver-backed evergreen foliage, and takes well to being clipped into a productive hedge or left more open as a specimen shrub. As with other feijoa cultivars, expect the best fruit set and size when a second, genetically distinct cultivar is planted within pollinator range, though established plants will still set some fruit on their own in a good season.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Feijoa Cultivar Selection

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Kaiteri sets a heavier crop with a distinct cultivar such as Wiki Tu or Anatoki planted nearby. Established plants tolerate brief dips to around 15-18F, making them reliable in zone 8 and zone 9.

directions: Kaiteri takes its name from New Zealand's Golden Bay coastal region, an area associated with several modern feijoa breeding selections, and produces medium to large fruit with good eating quality and the classic sweet, aromatic, pineapple-guava-mint flavor of top dessert cultivars. The bush grows vigorously with a somewhat spreading habit, filling out into a substantial evergreen screen or informal hedge within a few years if left unpruned, or it can be kept tighter with an annual light shaping cut. Spring bloom is heavy and showy, with the typical white-petaled, crimson-stamened feijoa flowers whose sweet flesh is itself edible. Full sun, well-drained slightly acidic soil, and steady summer moisture bring out the best fruit size and flavor, and mature plants shrug off the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers with little complaint.
sources: New Zealand Institute for Plant and Food Research — Feijoa Variety Notes

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April, or keep permanently potted and overwinter in a sheltered spot where winters run colder than zone 8. Bambina fruits more heavily with a second cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Bambina is a genuinely dwarf feijoa selection bred for patios and containers, staying only a few feet tall and wide at maturity compared to the 8-12 foot bushes typical of full-sized cultivars, while still flowering and fruiting on the same schedule as its larger relatives. Fruit is smaller than that of standard cultivars but carries the same sweet, aromatic flavor, and the compact form makes hand-pollinating or netting against birds far more practical than on a full-height shrub. Because of its small size, Bambina is an excellent option for Gulf Coast gardeners who want to grow feijoa in a container that can be moved to a protected spot during an unusual hard freeze, or tucked into a small-space edible landscape where a standard feijoa would not fit. Give it full sun, a large pot or well-drained garden soil, and regular summer water for the best fruit set on this space-saving selection.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Feijoa Cultivar Selection

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Waingaro benefits from cross-pollination with a distinct cultivar such as Wiki Tu or Kakariki for the heaviest crop. Established plants tolerate brief dips to around 15-18F, making them reliable in zone 8 and zone 9.

directions: Waingaro takes its name from the Waingaro district in New Zealand's Waikato region, an area associated with feijoa selection work outside the better-known Golden Bay breeding grounds, and produces medium to large oval fruit with sweet, aromatic flesh typical of the newer New Zealand dessert-type cultivars. The shrub grows with a sturdy upright habit and thick, leathery, silver-backed evergreen foliage that holds up well to wind and salt-tinged Gulf Coast breezes near the coast. Its heavy spring flush of white-and-crimson blossoms draws pollinating insects and produces the fleshy, sweet, edible petals feijoa growers often snack on before the fall fruit crop arrives. Full sun, well-drained slightly acidic soil, and even summer moisture bring out this cultivar's best fruit size, and mature plants need only an occasional shaping prune to stay productive and attractive as a hedge or specimen.
sources: New Zealand Institute for Plant and Food Research — Feijoa Variety Notes
California Rare Fruit Growers — Feijoa Cultivar Selection
